Entries.SourceTerm: 南來者與三十棒，北來者與三十棒

Senses.PreferredTarget: Give thirty blows to anyone from the south, and thirty to anyone from the north
SearchAliases: give thirty blows to anyone from the south, and thirty to anyone from the north
Senses.Note: Liangshan gives the same thirty blows to arrivals from south and north but says that even this does not meet the teaching. Langye insists the rule was valuable and repeats it without Liangshan’s reservation. Eryin finds both elders caught; Zhe’an compares their handling of students with two ways of ruling. Xiatang offers contrasting food, Songyuan waits until a student breaks through, and Wuzhun sets south and north arrivals to work. The paired blows become a measure of how a teacher handles a particular visitor, not a fixed prescription.

Senses.Explanation: Liangshan says he would give thirty blows to visitors from either direction, then declines to make that a complete teaching. Eryin finds both Liangshan and Langye caught in a trap; Zhe’an compares their ways of handling students to differing forms of rule. Xiatang offers food instead of blows, Songyuan delays the blow, and Wuzhun assigns labor to arrivals from each direction.

AlternateTargets: There is a blunt-nosed snake on South Mountain. Every one of you had better look carefully
SearchAliases: Xuefeng South Mountain blunt nosed snake watch closely

Senses.Note: Xuefeng's warning begins a case in which Changqing speaks of lives lost, Xuansha questions the need for South Mountain, and Yunmen acts afraid with a staff. Guting, Tianyin, Feiyin, and Sanyi each return to the whole warning and give a distinct current reading. Their comments turn the snake from a described object into a test of how the assembly responds. The exact words remain Xuefeng's in the quoted case; the later teachers are commentators.

Senses.Note: Xuefeng tells his assembly to watch out for a blunt-nosed snake on South Mountain. Changqing, Xuansha, and Yunmen respond to the warning in the old case. Later masters retell it, then ask where the danger lies and whether the old responses handled it. One says the whole earth is the snake; others warn that further explanations can themselves become dangerous.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 乃豁然大悟。拈云：益公道箇不知，果然親切，後乃豁然大悟，真箇氣噎殺人。舉雲巖掃地次，道吾云：太區區生。巖云：須知有不區區者。吾云：恁麼則有第二月。巖提起掃帚云：者箇第幾月？吾便休去。玄沙云：正是第二月。雲門云：奴見婢殷勤。拈云：糞草堆頭辯實，掃帚柄裏橫身，管他第二月、第幾月用得著，便用玄沙、雲門語裏有刺，是賞伊、罰伊？莫嫌霜露冷，添得好清香。舉：巖頭到德山，跨門便問：是凡？是聖？山便喝，頭禮拜。洞山聞，云：若不是奯公，大難承當。頭云：洞山老漢不識好惡，我當時一手擡，一手搦。拈云：問不在意裏，答預於機先，余所謂進得德山門，破得巖頭句，灼然兩彩一賽。洞山雖是善因而招惡果，又安知巖頭子為父隱，直在其中耶？鼓吹將來，三人綑作一束始得。舉：魯祖凡見僧來便面壁，南泉聞，云：我尋常向他道：空劫已前承當，佛未出世時會取，尚不得一箇半箇。他恁麼驢年去。拈云：魯祖見僧面壁，舌上有龍泉，要且不曾傷鋒犯手。王老師恁麼道，誠為善說法要。咦！舉雪峯示眾云：南山有條鱉鼻蛇，汝等諸人切須好看。長慶云：今日堂中大有人喪身失命。僧舉似玄沙，沙云：須是稜兄始得。然雖如是，我即不與麼。僧云：和尚作麼生？沙云：用南山作麼？雲門以拄杖攛向雪峯面前作怕勢。拈云：南山鱉鼻，毒氣薰人，當時若遇歸宗，免使雲門怕怖。然雖如是，還識今日遣呼者麼？舉鹽官一日喚侍者：與我過犀牛扇子來。者云：扇子破也。官云：扇子既破，還我犀牛兒來。者無對。資福畵一圓相，於中書一牛字。拈云：鹽官一條犀牛，侍者欄圈甚密，雖得資福牽出，繩索總在別人手裏。舉，仰山指雪獅子云：還有過此色者麼？雲門云：當時好。便與推倒。雪竇云：雲門只解推倒，不解扶起。拈云：五色令人眼盲，五音令人耳聾，既與眼對，便成滲漏。仰山指獅子示人：賣弄太甚，只饒推倒扶起，總在獅子上作活計。不受聲色者，知是阿誰？舉：法眼一手指簾，二僧同去捲簾，眼云：一得一失。拈云：明鏡當臺，明珠在握，照心徹膽，無有遺餘。法眼用在機先，者二僧一任指呼，且道孰得孰失？當衡者鑑取。舉：僧問護國：鶴立枯松時如何？國云：地下底一場懡㦬。僧云：滴水滴凍時如何？國云：日出時一場懡㦬。僧云：會昌、沙汰、護法、善神向甚麼處去？國云：三門頭兩箇一場懡㦬。拈云：護國三懡㦬，囫圇無縫罅，便是具鐵眼銅睛底漢子也分剖不下，惟同道者方知。且道

These records use the complete pair in public addresses rather than as an ordinary weather report.

Senses.Explanation: South Mountain’s turtle-nosed snake is a dangerous creature from an inherited Chan encounter, used to test whether one can meet a live challenge. Sanyi places the snake among other familiar encounter animals and asks what ordinary street presence can do beyond them. Zixian has it bite another named dog in a new verse. Tian’an asks who has the hand to handle the snake, then throws down his staff. Ruibai lists it with a fearsome iron ox before pressing what power his staff has. Daxiu says a barefoot walker who steps on it gets bitten unexpectedly. Baichi warns that a monk who meets it with light deliberation risks his life.

SearchAliases: the dream of the Southern Bough
Senses.Explanation: The southern bough is the records’ shortened name for the Southern Bough dream and its vanished dream-world. The ant-kingdom element is stated inside the corpus: Zhean Jingfan's verse says “the Southern Bough ant-hole—enter the dream and travel” (南柯蟻穴，入夢來遊). Baichi Yuan calls his hall activity “all one Southern Bough dream,” while Huqiu Shaolong speaks of getting free of it and seeing human affairs as empty. The name also enters encounter grammar without a story retelling. In Yunmen Wenyan's probing section, after calling an answer a dream, the record supplies several substitute responses, including the bare word “Southern Bough.” Dayu Shouzhi asks what his own dream-talk dreamed and follows with “Southern Bough, ten watches.” The Zen deviation is this compression and reuse: a literary dream-name becomes a one-word substitute response, the named content of Dayu Shouzhi's dream-talk, and a repeated line in hall addresses and case verses.

SearchAliases: two halls fight over a cat
Senses.Explanation: The public case in which Nanquan Puyuan cuts a cat in two after monks of the east and west halls fight over it. Nanquan holds it up and says an answer will spare it; the assembly gives no answer and he cuts it. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says his presence would have saved the cat. This written form occurs 128 times in 46 allowlisted texts, becoming a case title, public question, verse subject, and cited precedent. A question explicitly invokes the major precept against killing and asks why Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Jueyin answers a question about the case's import with ‘it takes Nanquan.’ Dahui Zonggao reports and rejects the inherited labels ‘timely wondrous function’ and ‘great function appearing without retaining rules.’ The entry preserves the rule, the question, and the rejection without inventing Nanquan's intention.
Senses.Note: The two written cat forms name one event. The complete event using expanded forms is family evidence; six exact witnesses across six sources clear the floor. Case title, question, verse, and later comment are deployments of the same public case. The precept-violation dispute remains unresolved rather than excused.

Senses.Explanation: Nanquan cuts the cat names the canonical monastery dispute and the decisive action at its center. Nanquan cuts the cat is the name of the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat, Nanquan demands a word, and the assembly does not answer. Later masters question, verse, criticize, and pair the case with Guizong cutting the snake, including explicit precept challenges but no single recorded explanation of Nanquan's intention. The wording functions as a case name, the object of public questions, and the subject of later verses and comments. In Miyun Yuanwu's recorded public interview, a question states that killing living beings is a major precept (殺生是大戒) and asks why Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake; Miyun tells the questioner to repent (汝當懺悔去). In a sermon for a newly completed animal-release pond, Guxue Zhe quotes the rule to rescue animals being killed and asks how the cat and snake could have been saved. Guangfu Weishang asks Jueyin, “What is the import of Nanquan cutting the cat?” (南泉斬貓兒，意旨如何); Jueyin answers, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui Zonggao reports and rejects two labels students apply to the paired cutting cases. Wuming Huijing names the cat and snake cases while discussing coarse conduct, and Shanyi Chun places the pair in a teaching-seat statement about cases and precedent. The entry preserves these attested precept challenges, questions, comments, and refusals and does not provide an unrecorded intention for Nanquan.

Senses.Explanation: This is the southern continent in the four-continent Buddhist world, often paired with other continents in Chan images of startling reach. Baiyu lets his whisk beat a drum in the southern continent while speaking in the north and moving through the other two continents. Zhuanyu names the southern continent while expanding the reach of an imagined ruler across several continents. Hansong places a hall address in the south and dancing in the north. Sanyi pairs communal work in the south with a drum in the north. Xiangya places horse riding in the south beside boat travel in the north. Wuzu Fayan includes the southern continent among four places he temporarily presents as Buddhas, then returns them to their own names. Yuanwu uses the name in a cascade of fantastical scenes, with the southern continent as one place in a much wider space.

Senses.Note: The phrase is a historical label, not two geographic essences.

Senses.Explanation: “Do not execute a defeated general” is a military verdict for an opponent already beaten; in Chan exchanges it commonly ends the contest with mocking or lenient restraint. Fenyang Shanzhao first keeps the martial frame explicit: a lone fighter cannot take up his bow and has lost his arrow, so Fenyang says the defeated general is not executed. He also gives the verdict after a monk's shout, hesitation, and bow, and when asked about Vimalakirti's silence, where no literal battle has occurred. Yangqi Fanghui extends it still further: when a visiting provisions master falls silent, Yangqi says the phrase and invites him to tea. The practical force is “you have already lost; no further punishment is needed,” while the wording remains the same military saying.

An exposed failure is a defect made visible in an answer, exchange, action, or speaker's handling of a case. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, attested), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, attested), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, attested). In one direct exchange an unnamed questioner asks, 'What failure do I have?' and receives the answer 'Wrong.' Elsewhere Dahui quotes Linji calling an old man's response 'a failure today,' then answers the question 'Where is his failure?' with 'The road is far and the night is long; stop carrying a torch, everyone, and blow it out while walking in the dark.' Yuan Cheng is asked how to have no failure and replies, 'Eat three meals.' A later comment can apply the verdict to both parties while also calling both adept: 'As failures, both are failures; as adepts, both are adepts.' These records leave the verdict attached to the cited exchange rather than supplying one universal defect that the word always names.

Senses.Explanation: In case collections and recorded sayings, an interjected comment (著語) is compact wording inserted against a cited exchange, often immediately after one of its lines and introduced by “appends a comment and says” (著語云). The Blue Cliff Record preserves Xuedou Chongxian's repeated comments such as “seen through,” and Yuanwu Keqin's recorded sayings insert “wrong” after successive turns of an older case. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly quotes comments by Yuanwu and then answers them from his own position. Tianyin Yuanxiu and Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise interrupt cited exchanges with short verdicts. A reviewed unnamed monastic questioner asks Langting Ting for a comment on a named case, while Xiangtian Jinian says he will place a comment against each line. The form can therefore name either the inserted wording or the act of adding it; it does not denote ordinary authorship where the verb authored merely precedes the noun recorded sayings.

Senses.Note: The line from the Faith in Mind poem says that clear, open awareness shines by itself, without forced mental effort. In a court dialogue Xiatang explains its older cited use as speech for someone who has realized the point; Shixi uses it in counsel about seeing, moving, and speaking without clinging; Wuming sets it beside several familiar Chan replies and refuses to turn it into a rule; Fachang voices it in a sermon, then asks listeners to meet the scene before them. Senses.Explanation: The smith's hammer and tongs supply a Chan image for forceful testing: the records pair their blows, pressure, and tempering with the handling of people in public encounters. The cited passages apply the implements to named teachers' handling, ask who has undergone their blows, and compare a furnace-and-bellows scene with the work of hammer and tongs. The image is attested; the entry does not infer an intention to transform a student's inner state.

“Test a person” means to examine someone’s capacity in an encounter. Songyuan Chongyue gives the clearest direct description: when a person passes before you, you know the person “to the marrow” before the mouth opens. Yuanwu Keqin describes Muzhou’s successive handling of a monk’s shouts and then says that at the exact point of testing a person, the response reveals recognition; this wording is Yuanwu’s commentary about Muzhou’s test, not speech by Muzhou. Xisou Shaotan says Huanglong Huinan established three barriers to test people, and Shexian Guisheng names a “barrier for testing people.” Jiaozhong Huian Miguang attributes an “eye for testing people” to Linji Yixuan. A later lamp biography narrates that Yunwai Xingze repeatedly raised the dog-no-buddha-nature case to test people; the compiler owns that sentence, while Yunwai is the person described. The term therefore covers direct examination, named testing devices, commentary on another master’s testing, and biographical narration of the act.
Senses.Note: The grammatical actor varies by source: a direct speaker may define or name the test, a commentator may describe another master’s test, and a compiler may narrate the act.
